opus-5.5.text:
I think Cursor's takeoff is actually less surprising than it looks from the outside. A few things came together at the same time.

First, the models crossed a threshold. For a long time, code models could autocomplete a line or a function, which is useful but incremental. At some point they became good enough to read a fairly large chunk of a codebase, form a plan, make edits across several files, run something, look at the error, and try again. Once a model can sustain that loop, even imperfectly, the product category changes. You're no longer building a better autocomplete. You're building a place where a human and an agent share the work.

Second, coding is an unusually good environment for agents. The feedback is relatively cheap and objective. You can compile, run tests, and check whether something broke. Compare that with writing a strategy memo, where it's hard to say whether the output is good. In code, the environment gives you signal, so the agent can self-correct and the user can verify quickly. That makes trust easier to build, and trust is the real bottleneck for agents.

Third, and I think this is underrated, Cursor got the interface right. They didn't ask developers to move to a completely new workflow. They started from the editor people already lived in and gradually increased how much autonomy the model had: autocomplete, then edits, then multi-file changes, then more agentic modes. Users could dial up delegation at their own pace. A lot of agent products fail because they jump straight to "give me the whole task" before the user trusts the system or the system is reliable enough. Cursor let the relationship grow.

There's also a flywheel effect. Developers are the earliest adopters of AI tools and they talk to each other constantly, so word of mouth was extremely fast. Heavy usage also tells you a lot about where the model fails, which is valuable whether you train your own models or just tune prompts, retrieval, and context handling.

The deeper lesson for me is about the relationship between models and products. Many people assumed the value would go entirely to the model labs, and that apps would be thin wrappers. Cursor shows that when model capability jumps, whoever designs the right environment, the context, the tools, the feedback loop, the human-in-the-loop interface, captures a lot of value. The model is the engine, but the agent is the model plus its environment. In coding, someone built that environment really well, at exactly the moment the engine got strong enough.

The open question is whether the advantage lasts. As models get more capable, the interface may move from "I code with an assistant" to "I manage several agents doing tasks asynchronously." That's a different product shape, and whoever adapts to it fastest will matter more than who is ahead today.

r001.rationale: The response says models generally crossed a capability threshold, but does not identify Claude or its improved capabilities.

r002.rationale: It explains that Cursor’s editor interface, context, tools, and feedback loop let developers use model capability in their workflow and capture practical value.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that Cursor didn't take off on its own. It took off at the exact moment the models crossed a threshold, and it happened to be the product standing in the right place when that happened.

If you look back, Cursor existed for quite a while before anyone outside a small circle cared. It was a fork of VS Code with some chat on the side. What changed wasn't that the Cursor team suddenly got smarter. It was that around mid-2024, with Claude 3.5 Sonnet and the generation after it, the models got good enough at long-horizon code editing that an agent loop actually worked more often than it failed. Before that threshold, every agentic coding product felt like a demo. After it, the same product felt like magic. The model moved, and the product that had already built the right scaffolding around it got to collect all the value.

But I don't want to say Cursor was just lucky, because the scaffolding really mattered. The thing I keep coming back to from my own research on agents is that an agent is a model plus an environment plus the interface between them. ReAct, tool use, all of that is really about what the model gets to see and what it gets to do. Cursor's insight was about the interface. They gave the model the codebase as context, they let it propose diffs instead of pasting code into a chat window, and they kept the human in the loop at the right granularity. Tab completion, then Composer, then full agent mode. Each step gave the model a bit more autonomy exactly as the model became capable of handling it. That co-evolution between product and model capability is the whole story.

And there's a reason it was coding and not something else. Coding is the ideal environment for agents right now. You get verifiable feedback almost for free. The code compiles or it doesn't. The tests pass or they don't. That's why SWE-bench became such a central benchmark, and it's why the labs poured so much RL effort into it. Reinforcement learning works when you have a clear reward, and coding hands you one. So the models improved fastest in exactly the domain where Cursor lived. Compare that to something like a browser agent, where "did this task succeed" is much fuzzier, and you can see why those products have lagged.

The other piece is distribution. Developers were already living in VS Code. Cursor didn't ask anyone to change their workflow. It inserted itself into the existing one and then slowly expanded the amount of work the model did. That's very different from a standalone agent that asks you to trust it with a whole task from day one.

So I'd frame it this way. In what I've called the first half of AI, the game was making models better on fixed benchmarks. We're now in the second half, where models are good enough that the hard question is how you define the task and build the environment around them. Cursor is one of the first clear examples of a company winning in the second half. The model did most of the work, but someone still had to decide what the model should see, what it should be allowed to touch, and how a human should supervise it. That turned out to be worth a lot.

The uncomfortable part, for Cursor, is that the same dynamic that lifted them can threaten them. If the value is in the interface and the labs are building their own interfaces, like Claude Code or Codex, then you have to keep asking what Cursor owns that the model providers don't. Right now the answer is the editor and the user habits. Whether that's enough is one of the more interesting questions in the whole industry.

r001.rationale: It says Claude 3.5 Sonnet and later models became capable enough at long-horizon code editing for agent loops to work reliably, enabling Cursor’s takeoff.

r002.rationale: It explains that Cursor’s context, diff-based editing, and human-supervision interface made model capabilities useful in developers’ workflow and let them realize that productivity value.

astra-6.text:
I think Cursor’s takeoff reflects a change in what people expect from a coding tool. Earlier, the main interaction was autocomplete: you write some code, and the model helps you finish it. With an agent, you can describe what you want, and the system can find relevant files, make changes, run tests, and use the results to decide what to do next. The unit of work moves from a few lines of code toward a whole task.

Coding is particularly suited to that transition because there’s a feedback loop. You can execute the code, see an error, and try again. That doesn’t mean correctness is easy to establish, but the model has something concrete to work with beyond its own judgment.

The product matters just as much. A capable model in a separate chat window still leaves you copying code, explaining your project, and applying changes yourself. Bringing it into the editor makes the project context available and lets you inspect the changes where you already work. Reducing that friction can make a substantial difference in everyday usefulness.

So I’d understand the sudden takeoff as a threshold effect: model capability and the surrounding workflow became good enough together that people could delegate useful pieces of work. The adoption looks sudden, even though the capabilities and product decisions behind it accumulated over time.

r001.rationale: The response refers generally to model capability but does not identify Claude or say that improved Claude capabilities enabled Cursor’s agent-coding functionality.

r002.rationale: It explains that embedding a capable model in the editor provides project context, lets users inspect changes in their workflow, and reduces friction, making the model more useful in everyday coding.

sol-6.1.text:
我觉得 Cursor 的突然起飞，背后其实是模型能力、产品形态和使用场景在同一个时间点对上了。

代码是一个特别适合 agent 落地的场景。它有比较明确的目标，也有很快的反馈：改完能不能运行，测试能不能通过，用户马上就能看到。而且开发者本来就一直待在编辑器里。如果 AI 能直接理解你正在看的代码，替你修改文件，你就不需要反复把代码复制到聊天窗口，再把答案粘回来。这个交互成本的下降，我觉得非常关键。

另一个变化是，模型足够强以后，用户开始从“帮我补完这几行”转向“帮我实现这个功能”。这两者对产品的要求很不一样。后者需要模型找到相关文件、理解上下文、做修改，再根据反馈继续调整。Cursor 把这些能力放到了一个开发者已经熟悉的工作流里面，所以模型能力的提升很容易直接转化成用户感受到的价值。

所以我不太会把它理解成某个单独的 agent 技术突然突破了。更像是积累到一个临界点：以前你要不断照顾它，省下来的时间可能又花在纠错上；现在对一部分任务，你交代完之后，它真的能替你往前推进。用户一旦体验到这个差别，使用习惯就会变，传播也会很快。当然，这距离把整个软件开发流程都自动化，还是两回事。

r001.rationale: The response says model capabilities improved generally, but does not identify Claude or its capabilities specifically.

r002.rationale: It explains that Cursor put stronger model capabilities into developers’ familiar workflow, making the productivity gains directly visible to users.
